video.title: The Most Overlooked Way to Make Money with AI (+10 More Ideas)

summary: Chris Koerner and guest Michael Girdley trade business ideas, then vote for their favourites. The pitches range from AI tools and localized creator content to physical kiosks, business marketplaces, investment funds, and speculative technology. The central AI opportunity is a service that adapts creators’ existing videos for other languages and shares the resulting platform revenue. Most ideas are brainstorms rather than tested businesses, and several depend on physical operations, regulation, or substantial technical and capital investment.

speakers.name: Michael Girdley
speakers.description: Business owner and guest in the idea showdown.

ideas.name: AI-content detection browser plugin
ideas.one_liner: A browser extension that flags online material likely to have been generated by AI.
ideas.customer: People who want to know whether online photos, text, or video are AI-generated.
ideas.problem: Users cannot reliably tell what they are looking at online is authentic or AI-generated.
ideas.offer: A browser plugin that monitors viewed content and flags likely AI-generated material.

pricing.notes: A speaker says they would pay this amount; it is not a reported sale.

ideas.delivery: A browser plugin passively scans content on websites and in inboxes and highlights material it judges likely to be AI-generated. Video detection is proposed as a future capability.

acquisition.how: The transcript does not specify acquisition. The plugin could use inbound content, app-store or extension-store listings, and paid promotion; human oversight would still be useful for positioning and trust.

onboarding.how: A user could install the extension and configure it in software, with occasional human help for compatibility issues.

delivery.how: Software can scan and highlight content automatically, but accuracy and coverage need monitoring.

billing.how: Subscription billing can run unattended through a payment provider.

support.how: Automated help could handle common issues, with human review for false positives, privacy concerns, and difficult cases.

uk_applicability.notes: The browser-plugin concept applies in the UK. Privacy, data handling, and claims about detection accuracy would need careful treatment.

risks: AI-detection results may be wrong, and a false flag could damage trust or unfairly label a creator's work.
The product would inspect sensitive browsing or inbox content, creating privacy and security risks.
The transcript does not establish that reliable detection across text, images, and video is technically feasible.

quotes.text: I would pay like 20 to $30 a month for this service
quotes.speaker: Michael Girdley

quotes.text: it watches everything I'm looking at and it flags for me stuff that is highly likely to be AI generated
quotes.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.name: AI-content detection certification authority
ideas.one_liner: A standards body that grades AI-detection products and licenses a certification mark.
ideas.business_model: Licensing fees from products seeking a grade or certification.
ideas.customer: Developers of AI-detection apps and services.
ideas.problem: Customers lack a trusted benchmark for comparing AI-detection accuracy.
ideas.offer: Grade and score detection apps against a benchmark and let qualifying products display a certification seal.

pricing.notes: The speakers mention yearly, monthly, or licensing fees but give no amount.

ideas.delivery: The authority would define a benchmark, test products, issue scores, and allow an approved seal to be displayed. The transcript does not state how testing would be conducted.

acquisition.how: Potential customers are software companies; outreach and credibility-building would likely require human relationship work.

onboarding.how: Applications and test submissions could be collected online, but test setup and scope likely need review.

delivery.how: Some benchmark runs may be automated, but defining standards and evaluating changing detection systems requires human governance.

billing.how: Recurring licensing fees could be billed automatically once a product is approved.

support.how: Certification disputes, benchmark changes, and challenges to a score require human review.

uk_applicability.notes: A standards authority could operate in the UK, but the speakers specifically suggest seeking an EU mandate. Government adoption and cross-border credibility would take time.

risks: The authority could lack legitimacy if it has no recognized independence or defensible testing method.
A benchmark may become outdated as models and detection tools change.
The speakers themselves describe similar certification models as potentially a racket.

quotes.text: some sort of a governing body someone to raise their hand and say "I'm the authority."
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Old-time photo booths in bars and malls
ideas.one_liner: Place vintage-style photo booths in venues where people want a physical, shareable experience.
ideas.customer: Bar and mall visitors, especially groups and tourists.
ideas.problem: People want memorable in-person activities that feel different from taking phone photos.
ideas.offer: A self-service old-time photo booth that prints keepsake photos.

pricing.notes: The transcript does not state a photo-booth price.

acquisition_channels.details: Get a bar owner on the phone and place a booth in the venue; malls and tourist locations are also proposed.

quote.text: you just freaking get get a bar owner on the phone and you go buy them from China or wherever and you place it that's it
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The operator sources and installs the booth in a bar or mall. Customers use it themselves; maintenance, supplies, and revenue collection are not described.
unit_economics_claims: A speaker assumes tourist photo businesses can persist despite high rent because he observed multiple competing businesses.
The pitch suggests placing a booth in a bar or mall at a lower cost than a tourist-area retail space.

acquisition.how: The suggested route is direct contact with venue owners, which requires a person to negotiate a placement.

onboarding.how: Site selection, venue agreement, delivery, and physical installation need human work.

delivery.how: Customers operate the booth themselves, but equipment needs restocking, cleaning, repair, and on-site oversight.

billing.how: A booth could collect payment automatically, but the transcript does not describe its payment system.

support.how: Equipment problems and customer issues at a physical venue need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: Bars, malls, and tourist attractions exist in the UK, and the experience is not dependent on US-only rules or culture.

risks: Rent, venue terms, footfall, and maintenance could make a location unprofitable.
The speaker's examples are observations and assumptions, not verified booth sales or operating costs.
Sourcing from overseas may create import, reliability, and repair challenges.

A prize mechanic needs clear rules and careful handling.

ideas.name: Minority-investment fund for small businesses
ideas.one_liner: Buy minority stakes in established owner-operated businesses to give owners partial liquidity while they keep running them.
ideas.business_model: Investment returns and a preferred return, with potential participation in a later exit.
ideas.customer: Owners of established businesses who want to take some money off the table without selling the whole company.
ideas.problem: Some owners want partial liquidity but are not ready to sell or retire.
ideas.offer: A fund buys a minority stake, such as 40%, and sets terms for preferred returns and a future exit.

pricing.notes: The speakers give illustrative ownership and business-size figures, not an established pricing schedule.

ideas.delivery: The fund identifies businesses, performs due diligence, negotiates minority purchases, and sets governance and exit terms. The existing owner continues operating the business.
unit_economics_claims: The example targets businesses with enterprise values of $5 million to $15 million and $2 million to $3 million in annual EBITDA.
A hypothetical example describes paying $6 million for a business and receiving preferred returns and a share of a future exit.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the model requires an investment fund and capital to acquire stakes.

acquisition.how: Sourcing owners and negotiating private investments depends on trust, referrals, and human deal-making.

onboarding.how: Due diligence, legal agreements, and governance setup require specialist human review.

delivery.how: The investment requires ongoing oversight of management, performance, and owner incentives.

billing.how: Distributions and fund reporting can use software, but returns and investor accounting need human oversight.

support.how: Owner relationships, governance questions, and operational intervention require people.

uk_applicability.notes: The concept can apply in the UK, but fund structure, financial regulation, tax, and transaction practices would need UK-specific advice.

risks: A minority investor may have limited control over decisions and cash distributions.
The speakers identify adverse selection and the risk that an owner loses motivation after a partial sale.
The investment can be highly dependent on the owner's management quality and grit.
No completed investment or fund performance is presented.

quotes.text: they're not ready to sell the whole thing but they want to get like partial liquidity and take some chips off the table

quotes.text: the smaller the business is the more it's wholly dependent upon the caliber of the management and the ownership

ideas.business_model: Marketplace fees or commissions; exact model not stated.
ideas.customer: Owners considering closure and buyers seeking an existing business, assets, customer lists, leases, or equipment.
ideas.problem: Owners may close without making a serious sale attempt, while buyers want a foundation rather than starting from scratch.
ideas.offer: List special-situation businesses and assets for buyers, potentially using an auction format.

price_points.label: Example price for an email list
Example price for an email list

pricing.notes: The speakers give examples of possible asset prices, not marketplace fees.

acquisition_channels.details: Find listings on BizBuySell that have been listed for a long time and invite owners to try the special-situations marketplace.

quote.text: you could get your first listings by just finding all the ones that have been listed for 365 plus days
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The marketplace would educate owners, publish unusual business or asset listings, and connect them with opportunistic buyers. Auction mechanics are suggested but not specified.
unit_economics_claims: The speaker gives $5,000 and $50,000 as example prices for an email list.

acquisition.how: A listings marketplace can attract inbound buyers, but finding and persuading owners who expect to close requires human outreach and education.

onboarding.how: Owners could submit listings online, with human checks for asset descriptions, legal status, and seller readiness.

delivery.how: Listings, buyer matching, and auctions can run in software, but special situations require human screening and support.

billing.how: Listing fees or transaction fees could be collected automatically once the fee model is defined.

support.how: Buyers and owners need help with unusual listings, sensitive business information, and transaction issues.

uk_applicability.notes: A UK marketplace for businesses or assets could work, but it would need to account for UK transaction, insolvency, and disclosure rules.

risks: Owners may be difficult to persuade and may have unrealistic views of value.
Listings could include distressed businesses with hidden liabilities or poor-quality records.
The marketplace needs enough credible buyers and sellers to become useful.

quotes.text: call it like an online marketplace like a biz by sell but specifically for business owners that have already resigned in their head to just lock the doors and walk away

ideas.name: AI EOS implementer
ideas.one_liner: An AI facilitator that guides a company's leadership team through the EOS operating-system process.
ideas.customer: Small and midsize companies using EOS or a similar operating framework.
ideas.problem: Companies pay costly human implementers to facilitate structured business-planning sessions.
ideas.offer: An AI joins a Google Meet, listens to the team, and guides participants through EOS steps using the book and templates.

pricing.notes: This is a proposed price, not reported revenue.

ideas.delivery: An AI bot joins a Google Meet as a participant, uses audio input and output, and facilitates the team's structured planning session.
unit_economics_claims: Human EOS implementers are said to charge up to $10,000 per day.
One speaker says he had been paid a couple of times to help with EOS and would accept $5,000 for a day.
The AI service is proposed at $250 per month.

acquisition.how: Inbound content and software listings could attract companies, but trust and adoption may require human sales.

onboarding.how: A company could connect its meeting and upload its framework materials, with human setup for its goals and meeting workflow.

delivery.how: The AI could follow a structured agenda and facilitate routine steps, but participants, conflict, and leadership accountability need human judgement.

billing.how: A monthly software subscription can be billed automatically.

support.how: Users may need human help when facilitation fails, the AI misunderstands a discussion, or a leadership problem needs judgement.

uk_applicability.notes: The meeting and operating-framework product could be used by UK businesses. The transcript's pricing and EOS context are US-oriented, and local adaptations may be needed.

risks: A chatbot may not create the accountability or authority customers expect from a human facilitator.
Sensitive company discussions raise privacy and confidentiality concerns.
The speakers note that some companies hire implementers because their leadership struggles to manage the process; software may not fix that underlying issue.

quotes.text: you're going to log in to the Google Meet and you're going to participate in this meeting and you're going to act like the impleer and facilitate us for the day

ideas.name: AI-first operating-system consulting and playbook
ideas.one_liner: Rebuild an EOS-style business framework around AI tools and automations, then sell a book and implementation services.
ideas.business_model: Book sales and high-priced consulting or implementation days.
ideas.customer: Business owners who want to use AI to change operations and reduce manual work.
ideas.problem: Existing operating frameworks focus on people and processes rather than putting AI at the centre.
ideas.offer: Create an AI-first framework based on first principles, sell a book, then help businesses implement AI tools and automations.

pricing.notes: The $10,000 day is an analogy to EOS implementers' fees; no actual AI-first service price is reported.

ideas.delivery: Publish a book and tools, then provide in-person implementation or consulting that helps companies apply AI tools and automations.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers compare the idea to a $15 book and $10,000 implementation day.
One speaker says the value proposition could be saving $30,000 a month in payroll; this is hypothetical.

acquisition.how: A book and content could bring inbound leads, but consulting sales and credibility-building require human work.

onboarding.how: A business needs human discovery to identify workflows, constraints, and suitable automations.

delivery.how: The pitch includes in-person implementation and replacing or changing business workflows, which require people and judgement.

billing.how: Book sales and consulting invoices can use software, though project scope and payment terms need human oversight.

support.how: AI systems and workflow changes need troubleshooting and human review.

uk_applicability.notes: An AI-first business framework could apply to UK companies, with changes for local employment rules, software availability, and business practices.

risks: The pitch does not explain how the framework differs enough to avoid copying existing material.
Promising payroll savings may be difficult to substantiate and could create customer or employee trust problems.
Consulting delivery is people-intensive and does not match an unattended-agent business without further productization.

quotes.text: there needs to be an AI focused EOS like EOS needs to be reborn a new company entirely but AI first
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Licensed adaptations of successful shows for new markets
ideas.one_liner: License a proven show or story and remake it for another language and culture.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; potentially licensing, production, or distribution revenue.
ideas.customer: Broadcasters, streaming platforms, or audiences in a new language market.
ideas.problem: Successful stories may have untapped audiences in other languages and cultures.
ideas.offer: License an existing format or script, then recreate it with local-language actors and cultural adaptation.

pricing.notes: No licensing or production price is stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Secure rights from the content owner, as the speakers describe the Colombian Breaking Bad adaptation.

quote.text: went and licensed the script to redo the entire thing in native Latin American Spanish
quote.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.delivery: Produce a localized version with local-language actors and cultural changes, then distribute it through an appropriate platform.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers describe the Colombian adaptation as made at one-fiftieth of the original's budget, without giving an absolute budget or verified financial return.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; licensing and production costs are not quantified.

acquisition.how: Content rights require negotiation with rights holders and often human relationship-building.

onboarding.how: Rights, scripts, cultural adaptation, and production plans need human review.

delivery.how: The proposed remake involves actors and film production; AI may assist but cannot remove the physical production work described.

billing.how: Distribution accounting can use software, but licensing and revenue-share agreements need human oversight.

support.how: Rights, production, and distribution questions require people.

uk_applicability.notes: The format can work in the UK, which has its own language and regional markets, but rights and cultural adaptation must be negotiated.

risks: The idea depends on securing adaptation rights; copying content without permission would create legal risk.
A successful original may not translate to a new culture or audience.
The transcript gives examples but no reliable revenue or production-cost evidence.

quotes.text: this format has actually this idea of taking something that worked in one place and putting it someplace else
quotes.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.name: Creator content localization as a service
ideas.one_liner: Use voice cloning and translated content to republish creators' videos in additional languages for a revenue share.
ideas.business_model: Revenue share on monetization from localized accounts.
ideas.customer: Creators with existing video content and platform audiences in one language.
ideas.problem: Creators may be missing audiences and platform revenue in other language markets.
ideas.offer: Clone the creator's voice with permission, translate and publish their content in another language, and split the resulting revenue.

pricing.notes: The speakers discuss a 50/50 split and a 20%-40% range.

acquisition_channels.details: Reach out to creators by direct message and offer to republish their content in another language. UK rules restrict unsolicited marketing messages to individuals and sole traders without consent.

quote.text: you go to folks who are generating content and say "Hey I'm going to publish it for you in a foreign language
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Download or use the creator's existing videos, translate and voice them with a cloned voice, then publish to parallel platform accounts and share revenue. The speaker proposes hiring offshore workers to run a playbook.
unit_economics_claims: The host says Facebook pays him $0.20 per 1,000 views on Reels.
The host reports that a Hindi-speaking copier had 400,000 Instagram followers.
A $50 monthly ElevenLabs account is proposed as a starting software cost.
The proposed revenue share is 50/50, with 20%-40% also discussed.
ideas.startup_cost: The speaker says a $50 per month 11 Labs account is needed; other costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: The proposed channel is direct messaging creators. In the UK, software must not send unsolicited marketing DMs to individuals or sole traders without consent; cold email to limited companies is a possible compliant alternative.

onboarding.how: With the creator's permission, a workflow can collect source files, voice authorization, language choices, and account access, with human checks.

delivery.how: Translation, voice generation, and publishing can be heavily automated, but translation quality, voice consent, cultural fit, and platform compliance need routine human checks.

billing.how: Revenue-share tracking can be automated where platform analytics and payout data are accessible, but reconciliation and disputes need human review.

support.how: Creators need a human contact for rights, quality, account access, and revenue-share questions.

uk_applicability.notes: The service can operate from the UK, and localization into languages used by large audiences is relevant. UK PECR makes unsolicited marketing DMs to individuals and sole traders a legal acquisition constraint; obtain consent or target limited companies through compliant channels.

risks: The creator must authorize use of their videos, likeness, and cloned voice; the speaker's phrase 'permissionless' should not be treated as permission to use someone else's content.
Unsolicited marketing DMs to individuals or sole traders in the UK can breach PECR.
Platform monetization rules, content ownership, translations, and account access can change or be disputed.
The speaker's own Facebook revenue and follower observations do not establish repeatable results for clients.
Translation or voice-cloning errors can harm a creator's brand.

ideas.name: AI-guided mosquito laser zapper
ideas.one_liner: A backyard device that detects and shoots down mosquitoes with a laser.
ideas.customer: Homeowners who want to reduce mosquitoes in their yards.
ideas.problem: Mosquitoes make outdoor spaces unpleasant and can cause bites.
ideas.offer: A device that identifies mosquitoes and fires a laser to disable them while avoiding people.

price_points.label: A speaker's stated willingness to pay 'a couple thousand'

pricing.notes: This is a speaker's willingness to pay, not a product price or sale.

acquisition_channels.details: The speakers expect a demonstration video to attract attention and sales.

quote.text: one Instagram reel and you've sold thousands of units
quote.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.delivery: Design, manufacture, and sell a physical laser device that detects mosquitoes and fires safely in a backyard.
unit_economics_claims: A speaker says he would pay a couple thousand dollars for the device; no cost or margin is stated.
tools: TED Talk demonstration by Nathan Myhrvold
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the speakers say the technology has not been commercialized.

acquisition.how: Product demonstrations and inbound online sales could automate much of acquisition, though a new hardware brand needs trust-building.

onboarding.how: A customer could install the unit, but safe placement and setup may require instructions or assistance.

delivery.how: The device can operate autonomously, but manufacturing, installation, safety testing, and repairs involve physical work.

billing.how: Hardware orders can be paid for automatically online.

support.how: A safety-critical outdoor device needs human support for faults, returns, and safe use.

uk_applicability.notes: Mosquito control is relevant in the UK, but local climate, product-safety rules, and laser safety standards would affect demand and design.

risks: A laser powerful enough to disable insects could injure people or animals, particularly eyes.
Reliable mosquito detection and safe targeting are technically difficult.
The speakers say this device has not been commercialized; feasibility and regulatory compliance are unproven.

quotes.text: somebody needs to build the mosquito death star that like sits in my backyard and just blast mosquitoes out of the sky
quotes.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.name: Laser-assisted tree trimming
ideas.one_liner: Sell or operate a laser system that cuts branches near power lines and other difficult locations.
ideas.business_model: Equipment sales, service work, equipment servicing, or licensing.
ideas.customer: Tree-trimming companies and property owners with difficult branches to remove.
ideas.problem: Some tree-trimming work requires expensive trucks and creates friction, especially near power lines.
ideas.offer: Use a controlled laser to cut selected branches, or sell and service the equipment for tree trimmers.

pricing.notes: The speaker describes a job price from his tree-trimming business, not a price for laser service.

ideas.delivery: A trained operator would bring laser equipment to a tree and cut a selected branch. Selling, servicing, or licensing the equipment are also proposed.
unit_economics_claims: The speaker says a recent tree-trimming job was $3,000 and took about three hours using a 60-foot bucket truck.

acquisition.how: Selling to tree-trimming businesses requires direct sales and trust-building.

onboarding.how: The customer needs physical equipment setup and an assessment of the site.

delivery.how: The work takes place in the physical world and the transcript describes an operator going to cut branches.

billing.how: Invoices can be sent and paid digitally, but job scope and completion need human confirmation.

support.how: Equipment faults, safety issues, and field conditions require human response.

uk_applicability.notes: Tree maintenance is relevant in the UK, but use near power lines and property requires local safety, land-access, and equipment compliance.

risks: A powerful laser could injure people, start fires, or damage property if misdirected.
Identifying tree species or branch thickness does not by itself establish that a cut is safe.
The transcript describes existing laser use in Asia but does not establish that this tree-trimming application is commercially available or safe.

quotes.text: you could sell the equipment to tree trimmers you could start a tree trimming business you could service the equipment you could import license whatever
quotes.speaker: Michael Girdley

ideas.name: Take control of a tiny county government
ideas.one_liner: Move voters to a sparsely populated, cash-rich county, win local offices, and direct public funds to residents.
ideas.business_model: Not a conventional business; the speakers describe a speculative public-finance and political-control scheme.
ideas.customer: Not stated; the proposed beneficiaries are residents and the participants.
ideas.problem: A county with few residents and substantial public reserves may have limited uses for its money.
ideas.offer: The hypothetical plan is to establish residency, elect a majority on the commissioners' court, and pass a dividend or other spending measure.

pricing.model: Not applicable; speculative use of public funds
pricing.notes: This is a thought experiment, not a business offer or a verified legal path.

ideas.delivery: The pitch involves moving to Loving County, registering to vote, winning local offices, and using the county's public authority to pass an ordinance. The speakers later identify physical-safety and reputational risks.
unit_economics_claims: The speaker claims Loving County had 24 residents, a $40 million-plus annual surplus, a projected $56 million surplus, and $200 million in the bank.
A $100 million dividend is posed as a hypothetical.
The speaker suggests three of five commissioners would provide a majority.
tools: ChatGPT (used to check the county name)

acquisition.how: The scheme depends on in-person residency, local campaigning, and political relationships.

onboarding.how: Establishing residency and voter registration require real-world actions and legal qualification.

delivery.how: Winning office and passing public ordinances are human political processes.

billing.how: Any public distribution would require government authorization and public financial administration.

support.how: Residents, officials, press, and legal challenges would require human engagement.

uk_applicability.notes: The idea depends on Texas county government, Texas elections, and a specific US county's finances and political structure.

risks: The speakers explicitly raise risk of physical harm from local residents and reputational damage.
The legal, election, and public-finance claims are unverified and may be incomplete or wrong.
Using public office to direct funds to a group of newly arrived voters could invite legal scrutiny and public backlash.

ideas.offer: Invest in technologies that make partnership, conception, pregnancy, childcare, tutoring, schooling, and college less costly or difficult.

tactics.name: Test a tourist experience in a cheaper venue
steps: Look for a physical business that appears to work in a tourist-trap location.
Test the same experience in a bar or mall kiosk where the rent and footprint may be lower.
Use observed customer behaviour, such as displayed customer photos, as an initial demand signal.
Close the test location if it does not perform; the speaker says kiosk leases may be month-to-month.

quote.text: take a business that thrives in like a tourist trap area and test it in with like a fraction of the cost in other areas
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Make a gem-mining kiosk visible and easy to trial
steps: Choose a high-foot-traffic mall location.
Make the activity visible to people walking past.
Price bags in the $35 to $45 range suggested in the discussion.
Consider a prize in some bags and display winners on a screen.
Check that the kiosk has a drain and an electrical plug.

quote.text: you could do like a prize thing where like one in 10 bags have a gold nugget or an Amazon gift card
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Screen minority-investment targets for owner quality
steps: Focus on established businesses with consistent management and double-digit net margins, as suggested in the discussion.
Consider a niche such as home services or HVAC, or use a longevity filter for businesses operating for 20 to 30 years.
Assess whether the owner intends to keep running the company after selling a minority stake.
Include management quality and owner motivation in due diligence.

quote.text: you want it to have been around for 20 or 30 years you want to see a consistency of management you want to see double digit net margins
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Seed a special-situations marketplace from stale listings
steps: Find listings on BizBuySell that have been live for more than 365 days.
Contact owners and invite them to list on a marketplace for unusual or distressed situations.
Explain that the marketplace is for owners who expect to close and for buyers seeking a starting foundation.
Allow listings for assets such as customer lists, leases, or equipment, not only whole companies.

quote.text: you could get your first listings by just finding all the ones that have been listed for 365 plus days and say "Hey we both know the score here come on over here."

tactics.name: Run an AI facilitator through a structured meeting
steps: Give the AI the EOS documentation and ask it to follow the implementer role.
Bridge the AI into Google Meet as a participant with audio input and output.
Have the team treat it as the facilitator and ask it to start the day.
Have it guide the team through the structured agenda and templates.
Add a human accountability layer if customers need more than process guidance.

quote.text: everybody would show up and then you be you basically treat the AI implement like it's a human being and be like okay like start us on our day
quote.speaker: Michael Girdley

tactics.name: Build the content-localization service around found money
steps: Start with creators who already have proven content in one language.
Obtain explicit permission to use their videos, likeness, and voice.
Create a localized version and publish it to an account for the target language market.
Offer to handle production and publishing in exchange for a 50/50 revenue split; the discussion also considers a 20%-40% service share.
Use a repeatable playbook and offshore staff for routine production tasks, with human language and quality checks.

quote.text: this type of model that works really well which is I call it found money where it's basically like hey like this is revenue you weren't going to get
quote.speaker: Michael Girdley
